rewrites.prompt: Namib Dairies has set the goal of raising its annual revenue by 25% over three years. Explain the difference between this corporate objective and a marketing objective that could support it.
rewrites.canonical_answer: A corporate objective is a goal for the whole business, set by senior managers - here, raising Namib Dairies' annual revenue by 25% over three years. A marketing objective is a goal for the marketing function alone, set so that reaching it helps achieve the corporate one: for example, raising the dairy's share of the yoghurt market from 9% to 13% over the same three years. The corporate objective is decided first and the marketing objective is derived from it, so if the board changed its revenue target the market-share target would normally change too.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - a goal for the whole business against a goal for the marketing function, derived from it.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the dairy - the 25% revenue goal and a marketing objective that serves it; 1 mark for a generic example.
Boundary: the difference stated on both sides, with the direction of derivation clear.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Windhoek printing company prints wedding invitations for households and packaging labels for food manufacturers. Explain the difference between the consumer market and the industrial market it serves.
rewrites.canonical_answer: In a consumer market the buyers are households purchasing for their own use; in an industrial market the buyers are businesses purchasing to use the product in what they produce, or to resell it. The printer's wedding invitations are sold in a consumer market: many individual buyers, each placing a one-off order at a displayed price. Its packaging labels are sold in an industrial market: a few large food manufacturers, orders written to a technical specification, prices settled by negotiation, and decisions taken by several people over a longer period.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - who buys and why: households for their own use against businesses for production or resale.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the printer - the invitations against the labels, with a consequence for how each market works; 1 mark for a generic contrast.
Boundary: the difference stated on both sides.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Windhoek hardware store sells the same 50 kg bag of cement to householders and to building contractors. Explain the difference between a consumer product and an industrial product, using this bag of cement.
rewrites.canonical_answer: A consumer product is bought by a household for its own use; an industrial product is bought by a business to use in production or to resell. The distinction lies in the purpose of the purchase, not the item, so the same bag of cement can be either: bought by a householder to lay a path at home it is a consumer product, and bought by a contractor to build a wall for a client it is an industrial product. For the hardware store this matters because it reaches, prices and promotes to the two groups differently - a displayed shelf price for householders, account terms and bulk prices for contractors.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - the purpose of the purchase, not the nature of the item.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the bag of cement on both sides of the boundary, with a consequence for how the store sells it; 1 mark if only one side is applied.
Boundary: the difference stated on both sides.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Namibian brewery sells a standard lager nationwide and a small-batch craft beer through a few Windhoek restaurants. Explain the difference between the features of mass marketing and niche marketing, using the brewery's two beers.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Mass marketing aims one standardised product at a large market; niche marketing aims a specialised product at a small, identified group. The standard lager shows the mass-market features: large volumes, wide distribution through bottle stores and bars, promotion through media that reach large audiences, and competition that turns largely on price. The craft beer shows the niche features: small volumes, a distinctive product, promotion aimed at restaurant diners who seek it out, a price that reflects the specialism, and few direct rivals. The trade-off behind both is that standardising makes volume possible, while specialising allows a higher price but limits how much can be sold.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - one standardised product for a large market against a specialised product for an identified group.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the two beers on matching dimensions - volume, product, promotion, competition; 1 mark for two unrelated lists.
Boundary: the difference drawn on both sides, with the trade-off between volume and distinctiveness credited.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A mobile network operator wants to divide its Namibian customers into groups for its data bundles. Explain the difference between geographic and demographic segmentation for this operator.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Geographic segmentation divides a market by where customers are - region, town, urban or rural area. Demographic segmentation divides it by measurable characteristics of the people themselves - age, income, occupation, family size. For the operator, a geographic split might separate Windhoek customers from those in rural Kavango, where coverage and usage differ. A demographic split might separate students from working professionals, who want different bundles whichever town they live in. The boundary is a fact about the place against a fact about the person: two customers in the same Windhoek street share a geographic segment but may fall in different demographic ones.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - place against person.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the operator's customers, with an example of each; 1 mark for examples without the boundary.
Boundary: the difference stated on both sides.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Windhoek supplier of solar geysers finds that households with the same ages and incomes differ sharply in whether they buy. Explain the difference between psychographic and demographic segmentation for this supplier.
rewrites.canonical_answer: Demographic segmentation divides a market by what people are - age, income, occupation, family size. Psychographic segmentation divides it by how they live and what they value - lifestyle, attitudes, interests. For the supplier, two households with the same ages and income sit in one demographic segment, yet if one buys because it cares about its electricity use and the other does not, only a psychographic division separates them - which is exactly the difference the supplier has found. The cost of that extra explanation is that demographic data can be read from official statistics, while psychographic data has to be gathered by the business itself.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - what people are against how they live and what they value.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the supplier's finding - the same demographic segment, different attitudes; 1 mark for a generic illustration.
Boundary: the difference stated on both sides; credit the contrast in how each kind of data is obtained.
rewrites.why: Distinguish is not used on the current AS papers; reworded to Explain at 3 marks - one difference, taken into a named business.

rewrites.prompt: A Windhoek bakery sells a standard white loaf through 40 shops and also supplies a gluten-free bread ordered by about 200 regular customers. Identify which market each product serves and explain what each choice implies for how it is sold.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the 40 shops and the 200 regular customers, not the business name alone.
Reasoning: the selling implications must follow from the market each product serves, and the link must be explicit.
Conclusion: each market correctly named, with a matching selling decision.
A two-part practice card: it combines an Identify part and an Explain part, so it carries no single paper tariff.
